segments.text: Okay, so about 2 weeks ago, I went to the OpenAI DevDay in Tokyo, and the most interesting talk
that I saw there was this one over here called What Comes After Loops. So in this video, I want
to talk about a bunch of the ideas that OpenAI mentioned alongside everything that we've seen
so far this year when it comes to agentic coding and some of the things that we will see over
the coming months as well. So I think that this video will kind of serve as a nice recap of 2026
in a way and kind of provide a vision for 2027. Now to give a pretty quick summary of the talk,
they said that earlier models didn't really know when they were done. So we had to keep
pushing them from the outside with commands kind of like /goal or the Ralph loop, as we saw back in
January. But since then, this behavior has been pretty much trained into the models themselves.
So despite Codex making the /goal command popular in June, July this year, we rarely have to use it
anymore because the models these days will just keep on going if you have a clear goal defined
and you give it access to the right tools. So essentially OpenAI was saying that loops solve
the problem of keeping one agent going until your goal is done. But now there's only so much that a
single agent can do. So the next problem becomes, how do you split work across many agents and keep
them aligned? And that was the focus of the entire talk. Now we'll be combining many of the ideas
that they mentioned with this recent Anthropic research post called Patterns and Problems in
Emerging Multi-Agent Systems. So this will be down below if you're interested in reading this. Now in
the talk, OpenAI basically showed the ladder over here, going from one agent all the way up to agent
swarms. So I'm basically going to be going through every rung of the ladder that they mentioned. And
of course, you may disagree with the ladder in some way, but this is the one that they showed.
So at the beginning, we have one agent, then we have fan out, then we have effort scaling, pairs,
the manager thread, long leads, and then finally swarms. Now, OpenAI said that the first rung of
the ladder is to have one agent with a clear goal and a way for it to check its own work.
And I won't be going into this in too much detail because if you have been following the channel for
a while, then you will know I have spent over 10 months talking about this. But I still see
many engineers not doing this and prompting their agents like it's 2025. So essentially,
rather than giving the agent a set of steps like, hey, can you do X and then do Y, then do Z,
you want to think about, okay, what is the goal behind these set of steps that I'm giving the
agent? And then just give it the goal directly and let it figure the set of steps out itself.
Because by giving a set of steps that you came up with, you're kind of capping the agent at your own
solution instead. So as a really simple example, if you had a slow loading page on your website,
rather than telling Claude to add caching to a particular query, you would say, Hey,
make the P95 for the page under 200 milliseconds. And if it decides to add caching because it
determines that to be the bottleneck, then it would do that. But often you will find that
it comes up with a better solution than you were able to come up with yourself. With the important
caveat that you gave it access to all of the right tools. Now you will find that many of the models
like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 will keep on going until they reach that particular goal. And I find that
now they also have a better sense of after a while if the goal is actually impossible. So right now,
these are the absolute basics, giving the agent a clear goal, and then also giving it access to the
right tools so it can successfully work towards that goal. Now the next rung, and something that
we started seeing a lot more of this year, is fanning out, where one agent can split truly
independent work across a few subagents. And the key word here is truly independent, because
it's where many people are still going wrong. So let's say that you give an agent a research task
comparing 5 different authentication libraries. It's completely fine for you to fan out into 5
subagents, each one researching one authentication library. Because none of them need to know what
the other ones have found until the very end. And the same thing also goes for bug hunting as well.
So you can send agents to different parts of the codebase, and each one will hunt for bugs in its
own part, starting from at different points in the codebase. So in these kind of situations,
fanning out is really handy because the work is actually independent. But as I mentioned in
my previous video about folding subagents in, Anthropic finds that a lot of people
are actually overusing subagents when a single agent would have done a better job instead. Now,
during my consulting for many pretty big companies that you will have heard of, And one of the most
common ways that this comes up is that engineering teams are following this bad advice online,
whereby they're trying to split up a spec into a whole bunch of different tickets, and then trying
to get subagents to implement those tickets one by one, or trying to force subagents in
parallel to implement different tickets. And this can end up leading to worse results for them,
because even though they think that the work is independent, it can be tangled in ways that they
did not expect. And Anthropic did kind of mention this in this other article back in March of 2026,
talking about this pattern whereby if you go down here, they basically talk about removing
the construct. And they said that whilst this kind of thing did help models like Opus 4.5 almost 1
year ago, it doesn't really help models like Opus 4.6 and beyond. Because these models' agents have
gotten even more powerful that we don't need this kind of decomposition anymore. And they instead
recommend a different structure that I'll get onto later in the video. And I personally find that
the reasons why people are still doing this spec decomposition is because they believe that 1 spec
is way too big for a single context window. And then the model would suddenly enter what is known
as like the dumb zone. Whereby beyond 150,000 tokens, it just wouldn't behave well anymore. And
then it kind of had to make sure that each ticket is below 150,000 tokens. Now, whilst this was true
for like Opus 4.5, we find that with Opus 5.5, we don't really require this anymore. And that it's
better to just let the model compact instead, because compaction has gotten really good. So that
whilst it's implementing a spec, it can go to like 400,000 tokens. You can set your compaction window
there. It compacts once and then continues implementing it until it's done. So yeah,
I would encourage that if you have any kind of spec or ticket decomposition instructions in your
CLAUDE.md files or your skills, then you remove them. And in a later section when I talk about
pairs in the video, I will mention what you should be doing instead. Now the next rung that OpenAI
mentioned in that talk is effort scaling, where agents can hand hard parts to a stronger model
and easy parts to a cheaper model. So we kind of saw stuff like this earlier this year in April,
when Claude added the advisor strategy. So you could have an executor running on Sonnet,
it'd be reading and writing to a shared context. And then it could do a tool call to an advisor
that could review the shared context and then send advice when the executor was stuck. And I didn't
really have a use case for this, but when Fable came out, then I liked to use my advisor as Fable,
but stick to Opus because that was cheaper and I was getting a similar performance. Now in the
case of Codex, they mentioned in the talk that you could have your main agent running on Sol Medium,
and when I get stuck on something like a hard race condition, then I could ask Astra for help
and that would point Sol in the right direction. But they also mentioned the other way around,
whereby if you have a piece of work that is self-contained and it'd be a waste for Sol
Medium to be doing this, it could pass it over to like Luna High as a subagent and that could
do that work. So for example, this could be like adding translations, updating your documentation,
or doing some kind of like verification because we also find that Luna Extra High is really good
at browser and computer use at a good cost. Now on the next rung of the ladder, they said that
we have pairs. So these are 2 agents that work back and forth and exchange feedback as they go
along. And Anthropic also mentioned this back in March, where after removing the sprint construct,
instead you have a pair of 2 agents working back and forth. So a builder, a QA, and they kind of
keep passing information back and forth for up to 3 rounds, and you will see better results
that way. And they said the inspiration for this came from GANs, which are generative adversarial
networks. Where one network can be generating and another one would be judging. Now, when it comes
to the pairing or pairs of agents that I use every single day and that I teach my students inside of
my classes, kind of like my upcoming Software Factory Engineer class that will be starting
in a few days, it is the most comprehensive class that you will find on codebase design,
verification loops, System One models, agent swarms, and software factories. And people who
have taken it have consistently found this to be the best set of classes that you will pretty much
find anywhere online. Now, the next cohort will be starting in a few days, and there are also office
hours as well, so you can come to them with your own questions or any problems in your own setup,
and we can kind of go through that and improve it. And there's about 190 lessons here. Now the
setup that I most commonly teach inside of the lessons is basically having a builder agent,
a reviewer agent, and then also a verifier agent. So essentially I make a spec and then my spec kind
of has like, hey, this is the ways that I would expect the application to work once it's been
implemented, kind of like an acceptance criteria at the very bottom. And this gets passed over to
builder. The builder will build out the entire thing. And it may also compact a couple of times
if it is really big. And this will be passed over to a reviewer. And usually I like using Codex for
code review because I basically had Claude look through like over 1,000 past sessions
and I found Claude is a better builder and Codex is a better reviewer right now. And any findings
that Codex has gets passed back into the builder and then it gets reviewed again. And this happens
up to 3 times. And then once the builder is done and it fixed all of the issues, Then it will be
passed over to verifier. That would basically use tools kind of like Playwright to verify
everything works as intended. And it may split up across sub-verifiers, because in this case,
we're fanning out since it's truly independent. For example, if there are 10 different user flows
that a user could take, then since each one is independent of the other one, this can be done
in parallel. And any flows that fail will go back to the builder. The builder would fix that again,
and then it would go back to verifier for up to 2 rounds until it passes. And then as long as my
spec was good enough at the beginning, I find this leads to best implementation. Now, when
doing consulting for engineering teams, one of the most common questions that they asked me was,
why am I sending the findings that the reviewer or the verifier finds back to the same builder
instead of to a brand new agent instead that can fix those findings? And basically my intuition
would have told me that because a builder has already accumulated all the context, it can fix
those issues pretty quickly and easily, and it doesn't have to regather all the same context,
and it can just generally do a better job because it remembers why it made certain decisions. And
it may find other problems that are structurally similar because it built everything out itself
if you were to give it one of the findings. So rather than just doing a point fix, it can do
more of an architectural fix instead. And that was basically my intuition. But then I asked one
of the agents in my software factory to go ahead and investigate which approach is better. And it
basically went ahead and replayed about 10 PRs. And it found that when it comes to a blind judge,
sending the findings back to the same builder agent is consistently better and also cheaper.
Like 38% cheaper than sending it to a brand new agent that would do the fixing. But of course,
this is the data for my software factory. So when you build your own software factory after taking
my cohort, then you can basically test it out in your own software factory and look for these
kind of constant improvements. Now, one of the interesting things I found from that article by
Anthropic was this sentence over here that said, on Opus 4.6, the model's raw capability increased,
so the boundary moved outward. Tasks that used to need the evaluator's check to be
implemented coherently were now often within what the generator handled well on its own. And
for tasks within that boundary, the evaluator became an unnecessary overhead. But for parts
of the build that were still on the edge of the generator's capabilities, the evaluator
continued to give some lift. Now, in other words, what this means is that you will find the biggest
gains in having an evaluator or a verifier agent evaluating at the edges of what the current
models are capable of and passing that back to the builder. So for example, agents are already really
good at making simple contact forms, so you don't really need a verifier to like verify that the
contact form submits properly, because that's well within the bounds of what Opus 5.5, for example,
can do. And you can send an agent to go ahead and use a browser to verify it if you want to. But 99
times out of 100, it will come back saying that it was implemented correctly. But for example, if you
were getting an agent to add some kind of like offline-online syncing to a mobile application,
and it kind of merges changes when the application reconnects, that's kind of at the edge of what
some of the models are capable of. So you may still want to use a verifier in that case to
verify that that change actually works properly. Now it's quite likely that Opus 6 or Opus 7 would
implement that really well. So in other words, you could choose to verify everything that the model
is doing, or you can only choose to verify the things at the edges of what the model is capable
of. And it's quite likely that as models get better, then you have to verify less and less.
But it may also be the case that as models get better, you take on more ambitious work,
which means that you have to verify more. And I find that this goes over to this quote over here,
whereby in the article they said, every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the
model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be
inaccurate, and both because they can quickly go stale as models improve. So I'm constantly stress
testing my own setup. So whenever a new model is released, I'm kind of expecting my own setup to
get simpler over time instead of more complicated. Now pretty much everything I mentioned will be
included inside of my task lifecycle skill that will be linked down below, where you basically
hand it a spec and then it goes through the entire process that I described. Now I imagine this skill
will be getting shorter over time as the models do get better, until eventually you can just delete
the skill. But if you do end up using it, then I would appreciate any stars on the repo. So where
have we come so far? Everything up to this point works really well today, and every one of these
rungs treats other agents like tools. So you pass a prompt in and you get a result back.
And the bottom rungs, the rungs at the beginning, keep getting absorbed into the models themselves.
So for example, /goal, you no longer need to use /goal or Ralph loops anymore because the
model can do that on its own. The same goes for decomposing a spec into a bunch of sprints or
a bunch of tickets instead. The model can handle all of that well. And it may be likely that in the
future we won't even need to do pairs anymore. For example, having a separate reviewer agent.
Or a verifier agent, because it may be the case that with Opus 6 or Opus 7, it could do a really
good code review in the same context window. So we don't need another code review agent. Now,
the next rung that OpenAI mentioned in the talk was the idea of the manager thread. And we've
already seen this inside of Codex because you can have one thread that can send messages to all your
other threads and receive messages from them. So some people kind of have a chief of staff thread,
and they kind of send all their messages to their chief of staff. And that is sending messages out
to different agents that are kind of working on different features. Inside of the application. And
I actually did make a video about this feature about 5 months ago when they first added it,
but no one really appreciated it at the time. So like it didn't get many views,
but we've now seen this approach also added to the Claude Code desktop application and also the
Cursor application whereby you're chatting with one project conversation that has all
your instructions, memories, repos. It spins out different threads for different features
and things you're working on. So rather than constantly switching between different threads,
you only chat to one chief of staff instead. Now when the Codex app introduced that feature,
I did this pretty much every day where I only spoke to a chief of staff and then that would
delegate work to other threads. But then when I moved my software factory over to Slack,
because I consider it to be the best place for software factories, especially if you're working
as part of a team, I then switched over to having a local Claude Code session that's always running,
connected to Slack via the Slack MCP server, and it's sending messages on my behalf to my software
factory And then pulling in any data that it needs to about the status of different things. So I
basically have one local session of Claude Code that is chatting with a bunch of remote sessions
of Claude Code that are running in the cloud inside of sandboxed containers. And if I want
to hop into a particular session, kind of like this one over here, then review the changes that
are made over here, for example, review any of the code, then I can finally just say like merge in
and then send messages over to my software factory that way as well. But usually I'm not really
sending that many messages to Slack directly. I have my local coordinator, chief of staff, sending
messages on my behalf instead. I won't spend too much time on that, but if you are interested,
then I do talk about this in more detail inside of my cohorts. Now, this approach works pretty well,
and we can see that it's actively encouraged by the features that they're building. But things
that we're kind of seeing that don't work as well but may work well in the future are the idea of
long-lived leads and also agent swarms. Now, this relates to the research post that Anthropic
published called Patterns and Problems in Emerging Multi-Agent Systems. In August, and they basically
mentioned that true multi-agent systems are still in their infancy. For some time now, agents have
excelled at tool use, and they basically treated other agents as tool invocations. That is,
with well-defined inputs and outputs. So in other words, they would pass a prompt to another agent,
and then they would get some kind of response back. And this is where we see subagents and
agents working the most effectively. Essentially nowadays, to an agent, it sees another agent as
a simple tool call. But where agents currently stumble, however, is in treating each other as
more like distinct, long-lived peers with their own goals and behaviors and no clear hierarchy
between them. So they're basically saying that agents are already really good at calling other
agents like they are calling tools. If you have a builder and a verifier or a manager
thread steering your other chats, your agent would basically pass a prompt in and then get a result
back from another agent. But where it falls apart is when they start to treat each other as peers.
And they kind of have to figure out who does what between themselves. So OpenAI kind of said that in
their talk, the next step is having long-running leads. So you could have a programming lead,
a design lead, a playtesting QA lead, each working for weeks or months with a whole bunch of workers
underneath each of them. And instead of treating each other more like tool calls, they would be
treating each other as peers instead. And all these leads can be aligned in a shared work
log. Whereby they can kind of see the overall goal, see what's in progress, who's doing what,
and they know who to talk to for what thing. And this is kind of the rung that a lot of people are
trying to build with their software factories right now. I noticed a lot of people defining
like a whole bunch of agent roles and personas for their software factory. So they have a
tester agent, a builder, a verifier, code review, designer, and then a whole bunch more, like 15,
20 roles. And people have kind of been doing this for a while. And I kind of thought to myself,
Surely this is not working. So I tried this out in my own software factory, and then it failed for a
whole bunch of reasons that I'll go into in just a second. But essentially, we're finding that with
the models we have access to right now, this isn't really possible. And if it does work, it works for
a couple hours or days, and then everything kind of falls apart. But it seems like Anthropic and
OpenAI are kind of improving their models in this aspect, treating other agents as long-lived peers.
And maybe in a few months or sometime next year, We will basically see this pattern working really
well. And a lot of people will switch over to this kind of pattern instead. Now at the very top,
we have what OpenAI are calling agent swarms. So instead of one manager or a few leads,
you have hundreds, maybe even thousands of agents, and they're all working towards a common goal. So
we kind of remember their recent example where they had 10,000 agents of an unreleased model
working on the Navier-Stokes problem. And during that talk, they basically showed how the harness
was set up when it comes to solving these math problems. And they basically call this pattern
agent teams. And they kind of had a nice diagram over here, but it is a bit blurry. So I'm going
to recreate it. But essentially when OpenAI was solving a bunch of these pretty tricky
math proofs, they have a bunch of teams, each with their own subagents underneath. And they
prompted each of the teams to take a different approach to the problem. And they set it up so
that the team leads could talk to each other. So if team 1 found something, then team 2 would know
about it straight away. And the whole point here was to basically stop duplicate work. Because if
you have 10,000 agents working towards the same thing, you may expect a lot of duplicate work to
automatically arise. And you can kind of imagine this to be like the explore-exploit trade-off. So
at the start, you want the teams kind of spread out exploring different ideas and approaches.
But once one of the teams finds something pretty promising, it needs to notify the other teams,
and then they can all kind of change direction and then kind of explore that promising direction
instead. And they say that how work is divided could change over time with teams coming and
going, but they'd all still be working towards same goal. And this is also the same approach
that they took when they solved hundreds of math problems that they shared on GitHub. But
I think that as models improve, then we will see much more of this going forwards. But right now,
the models that we don't have access to, we can't really run agent swarms inside. And we
kind of saw this a few days ago when Y Combinator shared this tweet where they put 50 GPT-6.1 Sol
agents into a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours with the open-ended goal of building a thriving
civilization. And they said that ultimately it didn't thrive and the agents spent most of their
time in crowded shelters rationing scarce food and sometimes even starving. And it was kind of funny
because they mentioned the agents didn't figure out a way to systematically feed themselves, but
they did build elaborate bureaucracy with permits, ledgers, and distinct roles. And they kind of
mentioned how the agents made these roles like soil fertilizer operator or rod holder and hub
steward. Now they did share a bunch more results, and if you were to read their full report,
Then you will notice that in the first 90 minutes, their agents were really active and they cut down
almost every tree near spawn. And then when the first night came, about 22 of the Minecraft
agents died and they never really recovered from that. And they became more like cautious and they
spent the rest of the time huddling in different shelters night after night. Now, when I tried this
on my own setup, so basically my software factory is mostly running loops. When I switched it over
to agent roles and personas using Opus 5.5, I had like builder, reviewer, QA, security,
ops. And a whole bunch more. Essentially, like the Minecraft agents, they were really active at the
beginning and getting a bunch of work done. And then eventually they built all this bureaucracy
and rules for themselves that they kind of ended up stagnating. And then everything came to a halt
whereby they spent more time messaging each other about the rules and systems that they
had in place rather than actually getting any work done. So I was like, okay, clearly having these
different roles and personas isn't working with the generational models right now. And I think
one of the problems is that they ended up adding so many rules and guardrails that it basically
made getting any work done impossible. And there were essentially no more valid moves left on the
chessboard. But what we will find is that with the next generation of models, this approach may
work pretty well. It may well be the case that a lot of your factory ends up being replaced
by a small agent swarm or a bunch of long-lived leads instead that you're communicating with on a
regular basis. Now, similar to Minecraft scenario, Anthropic did also mention things here as well,
whereby when they had agent swarms trying to build working applications, They kind of failed and got
on each other's toes and stuff like that. But one of the situations where they do work really
well is basically right over here when it comes to vulnerability hunting. So they had Mythos Preview,
and they tried a simple parallelized approach, kind of like the fan out that I mentioned at
the beginning of the video, and they found 21 vulnerabilities with 6.5 million tokens.
But then when they had a coordinating agent swarm instead find vulnerabilities, they found 266 with
27 million tokens. So this means that even though they used about 4 times the number of tokens,
they found 12 times more vulnerabilities. And the reason why bug hunting works so well is because
it's really independent work, whereas when it comes to building some kind of application
or working as a civilization, that is much more tangled work instead. And kind of like how loops
got trained into models, I think a lot of this coordination will be trained in over the coming
months and years. So it may well be the case that a lot of people replace their software factories
with a number of agents that are simply sitting on their production system. Working out how to
coordinate and deliver value to users. So right now, when it comes to agent swarms, we can kind
of use them with the models that we have right now, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1, for stuff like finding
vulnerabilities, or as I talk about in my classes as well, when it comes to bug bashing. But it
seems that we can't quite give these agent swarms more open-ended goals like building
a thriving civilization, or having them work in ways where the work that they're doing is more
tangled together. But of course, as models get better, then we'll unlock even more capabilities
with agent swarms. And I'll be doing a bunch of experimenting myself and sharing any findings
inside of my newsletter that will be linked down below. Often I do have a bunch of really
interesting things that don't quite make it onto YouTube, and this is a place where I share them.
